newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin vows to keep promises, but defers many.
newsitem.headline: Jospin vows to keep promises, but defers many.

text.p: Socialist French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin vowed on Thursday he would keep campaign pledges but dodged or deferred many tough issues like how to control budget deficits and qualify for a single European currency.

Jospin, swept to power in a parliamentary election upset on June 1, said he would give top priority to employment including promises to create 700,000 jobs and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 over five years. But he was vague about how.

"The commitments made before the French people during the campaign will be honoured," he told parliament in a policy address, outlining reforms ranging from making immigration laws more humane to closing a controversial nuclear plant.
Here is a comparison of Jospin's policy speech with his key campaign pledges:
EUROPE/PUBLIC FINANCES
Jospin reiterated that France was committed to taking part in the launch of the single European currency in 1999 but gave little indication of how he would tackle hurdles on the way.

He said France had won moves to put more stress on jobs and growth at this week's EU summit in Amsterdam. He did not repeat the Socialists' other conditions for joining the euro -- such as the inclusion of Spain and Italy from the start or that the euro should not be overvalued compared to the dollar.
He evaded the issue of how France would meet the criteria for economic and monetary union, notably the goal that public deficits do not exceed three percent of gross domestic product.
Jospin said he was launching an audit of public finances, as promised, that would be ready in mid-July. He said first signs were that the situation of public finances was "serious".
One central campaign pledge absent from Thursday's speech was that he would not impose any further austerity if cuts were needed to qualify for the euro.
He said the government would have a mini-budget ready in the autumn but gave no hint of what he would do if the audit showed that France was overshooting the three percent deficit limit.
WAGES, JOBS

Jospin earned low marks from some in his "pink-green-red" coalition including Communists and Greens when he said the minimum wage would be raised by four percent from July 1 -- far less than many left-wingers wanted.
During the campaign he had been vague about wage hikes for the low paid -- aides said he preferred to focus on cutting working hours with the aim of creating work for the unemployed.

Jospin said a conference would be held in September on wages, jobs and cutting working hours, over five years, to 35 hours a week from 39 but gave no further details. He did not repeat the campaign promise that the cut in hours would be made without loss of pay.

He said a plan to create 700,000 youth jobs was an "absolute priority". But he was vague about how the scheme would be implemented and funded -- during the campaign he said that a reallocation of existing subsidies would be sufficient.
PRIVATISATIONS

Jospin stuck to campaign promises, saying he did not favour privatisations of telecommunications, electronics or aerospace companies barring any overriding national interest. But he left himself a loophole, accepting the need to adapt to competition and to form partnerships with other European companies.
IMMIGRATION/ENVIRONMENT

As promised, Jospin promised to push ahead with plans to relax immigration laws and said France would scrap the fault-prone Superphenix nuclear fast-breeder and abandon the environmentally controversial Rhine-Rhone canal project.
